# Introduction

Every cross-validation (CV) estimate computed from MCMC draws has a Monte
Carlo (MC) error. The expected log predictive density of fold $i$,

$$
\mathrm{elpd}_i = \log p(y_i \mid y_{-i})
= \log \int p(y_i \mid \theta)\, p(\theta \mid y_{-i})\, d\theta ,
$$

is estimated from Monte Carlo means: the log of a mean, minus the log of a
mean, or the log of a ratio of means. The log of a noisy mean has both a
variance and a bias (Jensen's inequality), and the draws that enter the mean
often have a heavy right tail.

This vignette demonstrates the functions in the __loo__ package that
compute these MC errors for four ways of estimating $\mathrm{elpd}_i$:

| Method | Function | Draws needed |
|---|---|---|
| PSIS-LOO | `psis_diags()` | one fit to the full data |
| Mixture importance sampling (MixIS) | `mixis_alpha()`, `mixis_n_eff()`, `mixis_diags()` | one fit to a mixture of the LOO posteriors |
| Brute-force LOO | `brute_force_diags()` | one refit for each fold |
| CV bridge | `cv_bridge_diags()` | one refit for each fold and the full-data fit |

All functions take log-likelihood matrices with one row per draw and one
column per fold. A fold is one observation (LOO) or a group of
observations (leave-one-group-out), in which case the column is the sum of
the log-likelihood over the observations in the group. All functions return
an object of class `"cv_diags"`, described at the end of this vignette.

For background on the methods we refer to the following papers:

* Vehtari, A., Gelman, A., and Gabry, J. (2017). Practical Bayesian model
evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. _Statistics and
Computing_. 27(5), 1413--1432. \doi:10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4. Links:
[published](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4) |
[preprint arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544).

* Vehtari, A., Simpson, D., Gelman, A., Yao, Y., and Gabry, J. (2024).
Pareto smoothed importance sampling. *Journal of Machine Learning Research*,
25(72):1-58. [PDF](https://jmlr.org/papers/v25/19-556.html)

* Silva, L. A., and Zanella, G. (2024). Robust leave-one-out
cross-validation for high-dimensional Bayesian models. *Journal of the
American Statistical Association*, 119(547), 2369--2381.
\doi:10.1080/01621459.2023.2257893. Links:
[preprint arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.09190)

* Meng, X.-L., and Wong, W. H. (1996). Simulating ratios of normalizing
constants via a simple identity: a theoretical exploration. *Statistica
Sinica*, 6(4), 831--860.


# Setup

In addition to __loo__, we load the __rstan__ package for fitting the
model. The data come from the __rstanarm__ package.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library("rstan")
library("loo")
seed <- 9547
set.seed(seed)
```


# Example: negative binomial model for the roaches data

## Coding the Stan model

We use a negative binomial regression for the number of roaches, as in the
vignette
[_Using the loo package (version >= 2.0.0)_](https://mc-stan.org/loo/articles/loo2-example.html).
The Stan program has two additions, so that one program gives all the fits
of this vignette:

* the data vector `w` multiplies the log-likelihood of each observation.
  With `w[i] = 0` the fit leaves out observation $i$;
* with `mixis = 1` the program samples the mixture of the LOO posteriors
  that MixIS uses. The vector `mixis_alpha` weights the components of the
  mixture.

```{r stancode}
stancode <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;
  matrix[N, K] x;
  array[N] int<lower=0> y;
  vector[N] offset_; // offset is reserved keyword in Stan so use offset_
  vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] w;
  int<lower=0, upper=1> mixis;
  vector<lower=0>[N] mixis_alpha;
}
parameters {
  real intercept;
  vector[K] beta;
  real<lower=0> phi;
}
model {
  vector[N] eta = intercept + x * beta + offset_;
  vector[N] ll;
  for (n in 1:N) {
    ll[n] = neg_binomial_2_log_lpmf(y[n] | eta[n], phi);
  }
  intercept ~ normal(0, 5);
  beta ~ normal(0, 1);
  phi ~ exponential(1);
  target += dot_product(w, ll);
  if (mixis) {
    target += log_sum_exp(log(mixis_alpha) - ll);
  }
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik;
  {
    vector[N] eta = intercept + x * beta + offset_;
    for (n in 1:N) {
      log_lik[n] = neg_binomial_2_log_lpmf(y[n] | eta[n], phi);
    }
  }
}
"
```

## Fitting the model with RStan

```{r data}
data(roaches, package = "rstanarm")
roaches$roach1 <- sqrt(roaches$roach1)
n <- nrow(roaches)

standata <- list(
  N = n,
  K = 3,
  x = as.matrix(roaches[, c("roach1", "treatment", "senior")]),
  y = roaches$y,
  offset_ = log(roaches$exposure2),
  w = rep(1, n),
  mixis = 0,
  mixis_alpha = rep(1, n)
)

stanmodel <- stan_model(model_code = stancode)
```

All fits in this vignette use 4 chains with 1000 draws each after warmup.
The helper `fit_log_lik()` fits the model to a modified data list and
returns the $S \times N$ log-likelihood matrix. `extract_log_lik()` stacks
the draws chain by chain, so `chain_id` gives the chain of each row.

```{r fit-helper}
fit_log_lik <- function(data) {
  fit <- sampling(stanmodel, data = data, chains = 4, iter = 2000,
                  seed = seed, refresh = 0)
  extract_log_lik(fit)
}
chain_id <- rep(1:4, each = 1000)
```

The full-data fit:

```{r fit-full}
log_lik <- fit_log_lik(standata)
dim(log_lik)
```


# PSIS-LOO: `psis_diags()`

PSIS-LOO uses the draws $\theta^s \sim p(\theta \mid y)$ of the full-data
fit for every fold. The estimate is the same as in `loo()`:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_i = \log \sum_s w_i^s\, p(y_i \mid \theta^s),
$$

with the self-normalized Pareto smoothed importance weights $w_i^s$. `psis_diags()` adds
the MC error of this estimate:

* the MCSE of each fold accounts for the heavy right tail of the importance
  ratios $1 / p(y_i \mid \theta^s)$;
* the bias of each fold is the Jensen bias of the log of the mean ratio;
* all folds use the same draws, so their errors are correlated. The MCSE of
  the total takes the correlation into account.

```{r psis-diags}
psis_fit <- psis_diags(log_lik, chain_id = chain_id)
psis_fit
```

The `pointwise` data frame has one row per fold. In addition to the
columns `elpd`, `mcse_elpd` and `bias_elpd`, it has the Pareto $k$
diagnostic of each fold:

```{r psis-pointwise}
head(as.data.frame(psis_fit))
```

The five folds with the highest Pareto $k$ values:

```{r psis-high-k}
pw <- as.data.frame(psis_fit)
pw[order(pw$pareto_k, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], ]
```

If a `psis` object for `-log_lik` already exists, pass it as
`psis_object`. Then `psis_diags()` does not run `psis()` again:

```{r psis-object, warning=FALSE}
r_eff <- relative_eff(exp(log_lik), chain_id = chain_id)
psis_obj <- psis(-log_lik, r_eff = r_eff)
psis_diags(log_lik, chain_id = chain_id, r_eff = r_eff, psis_object = psis_obj)
```


# Mixture importance sampling: `mixis_alpha()`, `mixis_n_eff()`, `mixis_diags()`

MixIS (Silva and Zanella, 2024) draws from one fit to a mixture of all LOO
posteriors:

$$
q_\alpha(\theta) \propto p(\theta \mid y) \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{\alpha_j}{p(y_j \mid \theta)} .
$$

With $\alpha_j = 1$ for all $j$ (plain MixIS), the folds with a small
$p(y_j \mid y_{-j})$ dominate the mixture. Balanced MixIS uses weights
$\alpha_j$ that give each LOO posterior a similar share of the draws.

## Mixture weights: `mixis_alpha()`

`mixis_alpha()` computes the balanced weights
$\alpha_j = \exp(e_j - \max_k e_k)$ from the PSIS estimates $e_j$. It
takes a `psis_diags()` result or a `loo()` result:

```{r mixis-alpha}
alpha <- mixis_alpha(psis_fit)
summary(alpha)
```

## Predicted effective sample size: `mixis_n_eff()`

`mixis_n_eff()` uses the draws of the full-data fit to predict the
efficiency of a mixture with the given weights, before we fit it:

```{r mixis-n-eff}
mixis_pred <- mixis_n_eff(log_lik, alpha = alpha)
str(mixis_pred)
```

The output contains

* `r_eff`: the predicted relative effective sample size of the weights
  shared by all folds, that is, of importance sampling from the posterior
  to the mixture;
* `n_eff_u`: the predicted effective sample size of these weights for
  `ndraws` mixture draws (by default the number of rows of `log_lik`);
* `pareto_k`: a Pareto $k$ diagnostic of the prediction. Above 0.7 the
  prediction is not reliable;
* `ratio`: `r_eff` of `alpha` divided by `r_eff` of plain MixIS. A ratio
  near 1 means that balancing gives little gain. Balancing is the
  recommended default; the ratio only helps to save computation when the
  draws are expensive.

Here `pareto_k` is `r round(mixis_pred$pareto_k, 2)`, so the predicted
effective sample size is not reliable. We fit the mixture anyway and
compare the prediction with the realized effective sample size below.

## Diagnostics: `mixis_diags()`

We now fit the mixture with the balanced weights:

```{r fit-mixis}
standata_mixis <- standata
standata_mixis$mixis <- 1
standata_mixis$mixis_alpha <- alpha
log_lik_mixis <- fit_log_lik(standata_mixis)
```

The mixture can be multimodal, so MCMC can fail on it even when the
full-data posterior is easy to sample. Check the usual MCMC convergence
diagnostics of the mixture fit first.

`mixis_diags()` takes the log-likelihood at the mixture draws. Pass the
same `alpha` that was used to fit the mixture:

```{r mixis-diags}
mixis_fit <- mixis_diags(log_lik_mixis, alpha = alpha, chain_id = chain_id)
mixis_fit
```

The `diagnostics` element has the Pareto $k$ diagnostic (`pareto_k_u`)
and the effective sample size (`n_eff_u`) of the weights shared by all
folds. A `pareto_k_u` above 0.7 means that the estimate is not reliable. A
very small `n_eff_u`, for example below 10 with four chains, means that
the chains stay in different modes of the mixture. Compare `n_eff_u` with
the prediction of `mixis_n_eff()`. The weights of each fold are bounded
between 0 and 1, so the column `pareto_k_v` is of less concern:

```{r mixis-diagnostics}
mixis_fit$diagnostics
```

The realized `n_eff_u` is `r round(mixis_fit$diagnostics$n_eff_u)`; the
prediction of `mixis_n_eff()` was `r round(mixis_pred$n_eff_u)`.


# Brute-force LOO: `brute_force_diags()`

When importance sampling fails for a fold, we can refit the model without
that fold. The estimate is then a plain mean over the draws
$\theta_{-i}^s \sim p(\theta \mid y_{-i})$ of the refit:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_i = \log \frac{1}{S} \sum_s p(y_i \mid \theta_{-i}^s) .
$$

This estimate still has an MC error. For an outlier, the refit draws rarely
reach the region where $p(y_i \mid \theta)$ is large.

We refit the model for the five folds with the highest Pareto $k$ values.
Column $j$ of `log_lik_fold` is the log-likelihood of fold `folds[j]` at the
draws of the refit without that fold:

```{r refits}
folds <- order(pw$pareto_k, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
log_lik_fold <- sapply(folds, function(i) {
  standata_i <- standata
  standata_i$w[i] <- 0
  fit_log_lik(standata_i)[, i]
})
```

`brute_force_diags()` takes this matrix. The optional `log_lik_full` gives
the log-likelihood of the same folds at the full-data draws. Its largest
value bounds the tail of the MCSE estimate:

```{r brute-force}
bf_fit <- brute_force_diags(log_lik_fold, log_lik_full = log_lik[, folds],
                            chain_id = chain_id)
bf_fit
```

The refits have independent draws, so the MCSE of the total is the root sum
of squares of the MCSEs of the folds. Row $j$ of the result is fold
`folds[j]`:

```{r brute-force-folds}
cbind(fold = folds, as.data.frame(bf_fit))
```


# CV bridge: `cv_bridge_diags()`

Brute-force LOO uses only the refit draws. The CV bridge uses both the
refit draws and the draws of the full-data fit. It writes the LOO
predictive density as a ratio of two normalizing constants,

$$
p(y_i \mid y_{-i}) = \frac{p(y)}{p(y_{-i})},
$$

and estimates the ratio with bridge sampling (Meng and Wong, 1996). The
terms of the bridge estimator are bounded, so the estimate has a smaller MC
error than brute-force LOO when the two posteriors overlap.

Bridge sampling needs the two posteriors to have the same parameters.
Therefore, refit the model with the likelihood weight of the fold set to 0,
as `w[i] = 0` does above, and do not remove the fold from the data. In a
hierarchical model this keeps the parameters of a left-out group.

`cv_bridge_diags()` takes the same two matrices as `brute_force_diags()`,
but `log_lik_full` is required:

```{r bridge}
bridge_fit <- cv_bridge_diags(log_lik_fold, log_lik_full = log_lik[, folds],
                              chain_id = chain_id)
bridge_fit
cbind(fold = folds, as.data.frame(bridge_fit))
```

The `pointwise` data frame has two more columns:

* `gap`: the distance, in nats, between the median log-likelihood of the
  fold at the refit draws and at the full-data draws. A large gap means
  that the two posteriors do not overlap. Above about 50 nats the estimate
  can be biased. A fold with a gap above 500 gets `NA`;
* `converged`: whether the iterative bridge estimate converged.

The CV bridge has no detectable finite-sample bias, so `bias_elpd` is 0.
The `mcse_elpd` of a fold is well calibrated up to about 0.3.

If the two fits have different chains, give the chains of the full-data
draws in `chain_id_full`.


# The `cv_diags` object

All four functions return an object of class `"cv_diags"` with the same
structure:

```{r cv-diags-str}
str(unclass(bf_fit), max.level = 1)
```

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| `pointwise` | one row per fold: `elpd`, `mcse_elpd`, `bias_elpd`, and method-specific columns |
| `mc_error` | `mcse_total`, `bias_total`, `rmse_pred` and `interval` of the total |
| `diagnostics` | a method-specific list |
| `method` | `"psis"`, `"mixis"`, `"brute_force"` or `"cv_bridge"` |
| `dims` | the number of draws and the number of folds |

The `mc_error` element summarizes the MC error of the total
$\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}} = \sum_i \widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_i$:

* `mcse_total`: the MCSE of the total;
* `bias_total`: the predicted Jensen bias of the total, the sum of
  `bias_elpd`. The bias is a diagnostic only; the functions do not correct
  the estimate;
* `rmse_pred`: the predicted root mean squared error,
  $\sqrt{\mathrm{bias}^2 + \mathrm{mcse}^2}$;
* `interval`: an approximate 95% interval for the exact elpd, given as
  offsets from the estimate.

```{r mc-error}
psis_fit$mc_error
```

`print()` shows the totals and the first `n` folds. `as.data.frame()`
returns the `pointwise` data frame:

```{r print}
print(mixis_fit, digits = 2, n = 3)
```

Finally, we compare the totals of PSIS-LOO and MixIS:

```{r compare}
fits <- list(psis = psis_fit, mixis = mixis_fit)
t(sapply(fits, function(x) {
  c(elpd = sum(x$pointwise$elpd), unlist(x$mc_error[c("mcse_total", "rmse_pred")]))
}))
```
